alternative: Compose traits: a Scala class mixes in any number of traits (class Ball extends GameItem with Suspendable with Runnable), traits may carry concrete methods and fields, linearisation resolves precedence, and self-types (this: Runnable =>) express a required companion without a second object. Use a pair of linked objects only when two independent registries must each hold their own JVM object, and then keep the mutual references private and clear them on teardown.
idiom_name: pair of linked subclasses (traits that carry state and mixin composition replace it)
implementation_notes: A Scala class has one superclass but mixes in any number of traits, and traits may define concrete members and mutable fields ('classes can only have one superclass but many mixins ... the mixins and the superclass may have the same supertype'), so both hierarchies' behaviour and state live in one instance; linearisation decides which concrete member wins and self-types let a trait require the other capability without extending it. Simulating multiple inheritance with two linked objects therefore reintroduces the identity problem, the cycle and the manual forwarding that the trait mechanism removes. Keep the classic pair only where the two capabilities must be distinct JVM objects (two collections, two journals or actor mailboxes) or where a Java framework insists on its own base class and the second capability cannot be expressed as a trait.
pitfalls: Linearisation decides which trait's concrete member wins; two traits implementing the same member without an override resolve deterministically but not necessarily as intended, and the conflict is silent.
Trait fields are initialised in linearisation order after the superclass constructor runs, so a trait field read from a superclass constructor still holds its default value.
Traits that carry mutable state add fields to the class, which is where fragile-base-class problems come back if the trait is changed later.
A self-type is not a supertype: a trait requiring this: Runnable cannot be used where Runnable is expected, so API boundaries still need real inheritance.
